clue.text: Exist as greatest fan of 20? That's food for thought for him

definitions.text: That's food for thought for him

parts.note: to exist is simply to be
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen, cast by the setter as the most eminent devotee of the Morse series

explanation.surface: Who is the detective's biggest admirer, and what fuels his thinking?
explanation.walkthrough: ER (Elizabeth Regina) stands for the Queen. Inspector Morse (20 across) did his best thinking over a pint in an Oxford pub, so 'him' is Morse.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse claimed a pint of ale helped his brain work, so it was his mental fuel.

clue.text: Extremely old-fashioned police officer, quiet and somewhat eccentric?

indicators.note: the extreme letters, first and last, of the hyphenated word are taken

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector
sh is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: Describing an eccentric, old-school copper who keeps his voice down.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix -ish means 'rather', so a word meaning rather strange fits 'somewhat eccentric'.

clue.text: After service, set up ruddy odd and horrendous crime

indicators.note: the second part comes after the service in the answer

parts.note: Mass is a church service

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the words are written upwards, back to front

parts.note: ruddy means red in colour
rum means odd or strange

explanation.surface: After church, someone arranges a bloody, bizarre and terrible crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set up' turns RED + RUM to give MURDER; fans of horror may recognise REDRUM from The Shining.
explanation.definitionFit: Killing many people at once is about as horrendous as crime gets.

clue.text: Broadcast particular role — why is that significant?

parts.note: to broadcast seed is to sow it
wearing a particular hat means playing a particular role

explanation.surface: Someone takes a role on air and is asked why it matters.
explanation.definitionFit: This dismissive phrase is used to ask why something should matter at all.

clue.text: What's unusually true, say, about reading or writing delightful collection

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the single letter
unusually signals the letters of the two words are set in an unusual order

parts.note: reading and writing are two of the three Rs, so either gives R

explanation.surface: Something about literacy being made unusually true: an anthology of delights.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'three Rs' are reading, writing and arithmetic, so either of the first two gives R. 'unusually' makes TEASUY, which 'about' puts round R.
explanation.definitionFit: A treasury is a book-title word for an anthology of choice pieces, a collection of gems.

clue.text: Storyline showing reason for policeman's unhappiness under pressure

indicators.note: in a down clue, under means placed below the other piece

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure
Gilbert and Sullivan: 'a policeman's lot is not a happy one'

explanation.surface: A storyline about a stressed policeman's misery.
explanation.walkthrough: The line 'A policeman's lot is not a happy one' comes from Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera The Pirates of Penzance.
explanation.definitionFit: The plot of a novel or film is its sequence of events, its storyline.

clue.text: Criminal who does all he can to make a living

definitions.text: Criminal who does all he can to make a living

parts.words: Criminal who does all he can to make a living
parts.note: 'does' here means cheats, so this crook cheats everyone he can to earn his keep

explanation.surface: A hard-working criminal trying every angle to earn a living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'does' reads as 'tries', but in slang to do someone is to cheat them.
explanation.definitionFit: A con artist earns his money by cheating people, so cheating as many as possible is his trade.

clue.text: Part of religious education that's not new

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some school religious lessons are old material.
explanation.definitionFit: Something second-hand has already been owned, so it is not new.

clue.text: Contents of menu put away without a serious effort

indicators.note: the contents of a word are its inner letters, without the ends
without here means outside, so the eating word goes around the letter

parts.note: to put away food is to devour it

explanation.surface: Eating the whole menu, minus one item, is quite an effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside, as in old usage: DEVOUR goes round A. Morse's first name, revealed late in the series, is Endeavour.
explanation.definitionFit: An endeavour is a determined attempt at something, an earnest try.

clue.text: 22 down writer's pseudonymous first and real last name

definitions.meaning: the Oxford author of Alice wrote as Carroll, with this as his pen-name's first name
C. S. ..., another Oxford writer, wrote under his true surname

explanation.surface: A literary puzzle about an Oxford author's pen-name and real surname.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 down is OXFORD. Morse's sergeant also bears this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's invented first name, and C. S. Lewis's actual surname, are the same word.

clue.text: Ringleader facilitates unexpected visits by police

parts.note: the leading letter of the word ring
to facilitate is to aid, so facilitates means aids

explanation.surface: A gang boss enables surprise police swoops.
explanation.definitionFit: Police raids are sudden forced entries, surprise swoops on premises.

clue.text: Try nurse? 9, initially embraced, cheered up

parts.note: to try a case in court is to hear it

indicators.note: embraced means held inside the nursing word

parts.note: to nurse is to tend

indicators.note: initially takes just the opening letter of the answer at 9

explanation.surface: A patient trying a nurse is cheered by an endeavour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' is a judge's verb here, not an attempt. 9 across is ENDEAVOUR, giving E inside TEND.
explanation.definitionFit: To be heartened is to be given fresh courage and spirits, encouraged.

clue.text: Fatigue in the USA, possibly sign of times?

indicators.note: in places the multiplication sign within the rearranged letters
possibly says the letters may be arranged another way

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as 'times'

explanation.surface: Is tiredness in America perhaps a sign of the times?
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts X inside EHAUST, the anagram of THE USA signalled by 'possibly'.
explanation.definitionFit: To tire someone out completely is to drain them, the same idea as fatigue as a verb.

clue.text: Small section of church upset theatrical dame

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so read upwards

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church

explanation.surface: Part of a church is overturned for a grand actress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns SNAVE to give EVANS. Dame Edith Evans was a celebrated British stage actress.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Edith Evans was an honoured actress, famous for Lady Bracknell.

clue.text: Maintains page in novel should

indicators.note: in puts the single letter inside the rearranged word
novel means new, so the letters are given a new order

explanation.surface: A page in a novel says what should happen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts P inside UHOLDS, an anagram of SHOULD signalled by 'novel'.
explanation.definitionFit: To uphold a rule or claim is to support it and keep it standing.

clue.text: Government department's honour accepted by male, not reserved?

indicators.note: accepted by means taken inside the male pronoun

parts.note: he is the male pronoun
the OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour
something on ice is held in reserve, so off ice means not reserved

explanation.surface: A ministry's award goes to a man who is open, not reserved.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Office is the UK ministry for policing and immigration. 'department's' carries 's for 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Home Office is a British ministry of state, handling policing and borders.

clue.text: Weapon and drug stored in box

indicators.note: stored in means placed inside the boxing word

parts.note: to box is to spar
E is ecstasy, the drug

explanation.surface: A weapon and narcotics hidden in a crate.
explanation.definitionFit: A spear is a long thrusting or throwing arm with a pointed head.

clue.text: Something don may have done that contains one bug

indicators.note: contains means the doctorate holds the number one inside

parts.note: a university don may have a PhD, a doctorate
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An academic's work contains one error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bug' looks like a software fault next to academic work, but it is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: This greenfly is a small sap-sucking insect, and bug is a loose word for an insect.

clue.text: Playwright's wife isn't lacking technique, though dated

parts.note: isn't lacking means has, in the archaic form 'hath', as 'though dated' says
a way of doing something is a technique

explanation.surface: A spouse with old-fashioned but real skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'though dated' tells you to use the old form of 'has'. Anne Hathaway married Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Hathaway was Shakespeare's wife, the most famous dramatist's spouse.

clue.text: See final bits of The Remorseful Day

indicators.note: the final bits of the words are their last letters

explanation.surface: Look at the ending of the last Morse novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Remorseful Day is the final Inspector Morse novel. 'See' is a bishop's diocese, not 'look'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ely is a cathedral city and the seat of a bishop, a diocese or see.

clue.text: Ruminate, getting stuck into ales, perhaps — avoidance behaviour?

indicators.note: stuck into means put inside the rearranged letters
perhaps says the letters may be put in another order

parts.note: to ruminate is to chew the cud

explanation.surface: Mulling things over while getting stuck into the beer: a way of avoiding things?
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' makes ESAL from the drinks, and 'stuck into' places the cud-chewing word inside it; 'ales' looks like Morse's beer but is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To eschew is to shun or abstain, so the noun means the act of steering clear.

clue.text: Form of communication that's a little bit incomplete

indicators.note: incomplete means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a morsel is a little bit, of food especially

explanation.surface: A way of talking that isn't quite whole.
explanation.walkthrough: The theme detective's name is also the dot-and-dash telegraph code.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Morse's code of dots and dashes is a signalling system for messages.

clue.text: Try, as arranged, one caught being excessively lustful

indicators.note: arranged says the letters are put in a fresh order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Someone trying, as planned, gets caught for lechery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' rearranges TRY AS to give SATYR, the goat-like lecher of myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Satyrs in Greek myth were lecherous woodland creatures, so the adjective means lecherous.

clue.text: Like something requested relating to Freemasons, say

definitions.note: goods requested but not yet delivered are said to be awaiting delivery

parts.note: on means about or concerning
the Freemasons are an example of a fraternal order

explanation.surface: Describing a request concerning the Freemasons.
explanation.walkthrough: Freemasonry featured in several Morse plots.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods requested from a supplier and still awaited are described with this phrase.

clue.text: Not totally orthodox for detective that embraces lost causes

indicators.note: not totally means only part of the words is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: An unorthodox detective who champions hopeless causes.
explanation.walkthrough: Matthew Arnold called Oxford the 'home of lost causes'; it is Morse's city.
explanation.definitionFit: The university city was famously called the home of lost causes by Matthew Arnold.

clue.text: Stop vote being held that's historically right

indicators.note: being held means the vote mark sits inside the stopping word

parts.note: to deter is to stop or discourage
a cross, X, marks a vote on a ballot

explanation.surface: Preventing a vote that was right in former times.
explanation.walkthrough: Colin Dexter created Morse. In heraldry and old usage this word means the right-hand side.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin-derived term for right-hand was used in older English and still in heraldry.

clue.text: Fare to be cooked over first part of Sunday?

definitions.text: Fare to be cooked over first part of Sunday?

indicators.note: over means the rearranged letters cover the single letter
cooked signals the letters are mixed up, as ingredients are
the first part of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Food prepared at the start of a Sunday: the traditional British Sunday roast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' puts the anagram ROATBEEF, made by 'cooked' from FARE TO BE, around S.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint served for Sunday lunch in Britain is classically this meat.

clue.text: Annoyed, getting answer to crossword clue, finally

indicators.note: finally takes the final letter of each word

explanation.surface: Irritated at finally getting a crossword answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ride someone is to nag or harass them, so being ridden is being bothered.

clue.text: What changed as one result of global warming

indicators.note: changed signals the letters of the word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asking what has changed due to climate warming.
explanation.definitionFit: Rising temperatures melt ice and snow, an obvious consequence of warming.

clue.text: Like page spotted in old book, was baffling

definitions.text: Like page spotted in old book
definitions.meaning: old paper gets brownish spots with age, called foxing
to fox is to baffle or puzzle

explanation.surface: A puzzling stain on a page of an old volume.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses use the verb fox: to stain with brown spots, and to puzzle.

clue.text: Verve shown in part of 20

definitions.meaning: verve is flair or spirited style
20 is the dot-and-... signalling code, whose long signal is a stroke

explanation.surface: Panache seen in a bit of a code.
explanation.definitionFit: Energetic style is panache, and the long signal of telegraph code is the other sense.

clue.text: Exciting series of events — a little drink leads to answer

parts.note: a dram is a small measure of whisky

explanation.surface: A tot of whisky leads to an answer, Morse-style.
explanation.definitionFit: A tense run of events is called a drama, as on stage.

clue.text: Teams operating planes without second propellers

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the teams go around the letter

parts.note: aircrews are the teams that fly aircraft

explanation.surface: Flight teams struggling without a second set of propellers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside, so AIRCREWS goes around S.
explanation.definitionFit: Aircraft propellers are known as airscrews, especially in British usage.
